title: 30-minute Screening Simulation
description: A first-round screening simulation: 10 rapid questions across quick coding-output, probability, C++ and finance. It deliberately simulates the time pressure of a real screening call - about 3 minutes per question, no partial credit for rough working, and the clock is part of the test. Real first rounds are scored on pace and accuracy under pressure as much as on depth: if a question stalls you past ~3 minutes, commit to your best guess and move on. Exactly the mix and tempo you should expect when a phone screen turns to mental math and code reading.

questions.prompt: What does this Python code print? (Answer fast - this is a screening.)
questions.code:
s = 0
for i in range(3, 8):
    s += i
print(s)
questions.explanation: range(3, 8) is 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 (endpoint exclusive): $3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 25$. Screening tip: sum the pair extremes (3+7, 4+6, 5) = 10 + 10 + 5.

questions.prompt: What does this Python code print?
questions.explanation: Assignment copies the REFERENCE, not the list: a and b point to the same object, so appending via b is visible through a - length 4. Screening interviewers use this to check you model Python's object semantics, not C-style value copy.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. What is the probability of exactly 2 heads? (Decimal or fraction-as-decimal.)
questions.explanation: $\binom{3}{2}/2^3 = 3/8 = 0.375$: the favourable sequences are HHT, HTH, THH. Count-then-scale is faster than any formula here.

questions.prompt: What is the expected sum of two fair six-sided dice?
questions.explanation: Linearity: $E[X_1 + X_2] = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7$. Memorise the die mean (3.5) and the two-dice sum distribution (peaked at 7) - both appear in screens constantly.

questions.prompt: In C++: `void f(std::string s);` is called as `f(name);` where `std::string name = "quant";`. What happens?
options: name is copied into the parameter s
name is moved into the parameter s
s references name's memory - no copy occurs
Compilation error: passing an lvalue to a by-value parameter is illegal
questions.explanation: Passing an lvalue to a by-value parameter invokes the copy constructor (it cannot move, because the caller's object must stay valid). Only an rvalue argument - a temporary, or std::move(name) - selects the move constructor. This is the core of move-semantics screening questions.

questions.prompt: In C++: `uint8_t x = 200; int y = x + 100;` What is the value of y?
questions.explanation: uint8_t is promoted to int before the addition, so the arithmetic happens in (at least) 32-bit signed int: $200 + 100 = 300$, no wraparound. It would wrap to 44 only if the result were assigned back to a uint8_t ($300 \bmod 256 = 44$). Integer promotion is the screening favourite behind most 'surprising' C++ arithmetic.

questions.prompt: You buy 100 shares at \$25.50 and sell all 100 at \$26.20 (no commissions). What is your total PnL in dollars?
questions.explanation: Per share: $26.20 - 25.50 = 0.70$. Total: $100 \times 0.70 = 70$. Screens often use per-share-then-scale because it is faster and less error-prone than multiplying two 4-digit numbers first.

questions.prompt: A 1-year zero-coupon bond has a face value of \$100 and a yield of 4%. What is its price today? (Decimal to 2 places.)
questions.explanation: $100 / 1.04 = 96.1538 \approx 96.15$. One division - and the same discounting principle extends to every fixed-income price in the interview loop.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. You are told the sum is 8. What is the probability that at least one die shows a 6? (Decimal to 3-4 significant figures.)
questions.explanation: Sum-8 outcomes: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) - five equally likely cases, of which two contain a 6. So $P = 2/5 = 0.4$. The screening skill is enumerating the CONDITIONED sample space instead of computing unconditional probabilities and trying to adjust them.

questions.prompt: Last one - what does this Python code print?
questions.explanation: The loop counts occurrences: bb appears twice, aa twice, cc once - d = {'bb': 2, 'aa': 2, 'cc': 1}. Then $d.get("bb") + d.get("cc") = 2 + 1 = 3$. The dict.get(key, default) counting idiom is worth having cold; fumbling it on a screen burns 90 seconds you do not have.
